lines.text: A Farmacy Food customer arrives at the fridge to pick up their meal, and right at that moment the fridge has no network. It cannot check online who that person is or what they bought. And what the business sells is, precisely, that the customer leaves with their meal.

The team's answer was a code. Every meal that leaves the kitchen carries a code of six to eight digits, generated in advance. It is sent early to the fridge and to the customer's phone, while there is network. If the network drops later, the fridge compares the code with what it has in its memory and opens anyway.

The team also noted what that brings. Someone very lucky could guess a code on the first try, and eight digits are already awkward to type. And it noted an advantage that came as a bonus, that sending someone else to pick up the meal becomes easy.
When something fails, the first question is what the business cannot lose. The rest can fail for a while without anything serious happening. To protect what cannot be lost there are four families.

The first is a second path, another copy or another channel that keeps going if the first one falls. It gains because one piece failing does not cut the service. It pays with twice as many things to maintain.

The second is carrying on without the other side, like the fridge that opens with no network. It gains because the essential keeps working. It pays with work beforehand, because what is needed has to be in place before the failure.

The third is retrying. What failed is kept in a queue and tried again later. It gains because a passing failure loses nothing. It pays with delays, and with the same thing possibly arriving more than once.

The fourth is making repeats harmless. Each message carries something to recognize it by, and whoever receives it discards the one it already processed. It gains with correct data even when messages repeat. It pays with some performance and with pieces that keep count.
At MonitorMe, what cannot fail is the alert. If a patient gets worse, someone has to find out. The team wrote that, in this system, the priority is people's lives.

So the alert goes out by two different paths. One sends a notification to the medical staff's phone, over the internet. The other shows it on the screen at the nurses' station, over the hospital's local network. If one of the two is not available, the warning goes out anyway through the other.
The cost of the two paths is in the decision too. They are two forms of communication to maintain, with the data in the same format in both, and both have to be watched so they keep working.

Farmacy Food and MonitorMe protect what their business cannot lose, with two different families. Farmacy Food needs the customer to leave with their meal, and gets it with a fridge that carries on without network. MonitorMe needs the doctor to find out, and gets it with a second path. Both started by asking what happens if this fails, before it failed.

ClearView has a hard edge. When a company unlocks a candidate, the résumé has to reach that company's human resources system. There are about a hundred different systems, with thousands of configurations, and the team wrote that failures will be an everyday thing.

The first thing it decided was that a human resources system being down blocks nothing. The sending does not wait for the answer, and a separate service does it. If a sending fails, it goes to a queue of failed ones, and that queue is tried again every so often. To avoid spending too much, the team notes that it can wait a little longer each time between one attempt and the next.

Retrying brings its own problem. To avoid losing a message, the queue waits for whoever processes it to say it finished, and if that notice does not arrive, it delivers it again. But the notice can also get lost, even though the work was already done. That way, the same message arrives twice.

At Farmacy Food, the message that cannot be lost is the ready-to-pay order, and what cannot be repeated is the charge. The team proposes that the order travel with a unique identifier, generated by the customer's phone, and with a version number. If an order arrives with an identifier and a version already processed, it is discarded. The cost fits in one line, a little less performance in exchange for correct data.

There is another way to end up halfway. When something happens in the business, the system has to store it in its database and also tell the other parts. They are two writes, and if the system goes down between one and the other, the database says one thing and the rest never finds out.

Farmacy Family, the second phase of the same business, solved it with two boxes. When announcing, the event is first stored in the same database, in an outbox, and another process sends it and marks it as sent. When receiving, the event goes into an inbox, and another process handles it and marks it as handled. That way, if it arrives twice, the second one is ignored. The price is more complexity, with separate processes that check the boxes.

In the face of any possible failure, the question is what the business cannot lose, and what happens if this fails. If there cannot be a single outage, a second path is needed. If what is outside is unreliable, it pays to be able to carry on without it. And if what matters is that it arrives even if late, you retry, making sure that repeating does no harm.
